description: The child, named Margaret, is described as having black, rich eyes with a deep sense of superior knowledge, appearing above the knowledge of evil and evoking both trust and discomfort in Rags. She strokes Rags’s cheek, smiles with confidence and tenderness, and hugs him tightly, creating an oppressive silence between them. Rags feels a mix of pleasure and unease, whispering he wanted to kill her, yet she remains calm and unresponsive to his words. The bishop is deeply serious about the child, viewing her as his only child and believing his duty extends beyond basic care. A man in the scene insists on being shot, claiming he has served his time and cannot hurt anyone due to suffering from prison, with his face and hair showing his past. The setting is cold and bleak, with Rags trembling from the rain and sleet, and both the man and child sleeping in a dark tenement corner.

The Goodwood Plunger is a figure marked by introspection and emotional strain, experiencing physical tremors and a persistent pain that is no longer a matter of inclination. He turns away from lights and tears up a letter, whispering a desire to stop thoughts and anxiety, and expresses irritation toward a woman who approaches him, stating she is in great trouble, bold, and anxious. He had prior interactions with women who lost at the tables in Monte Carlo, where they sought advice or a napoleon, which once amused him, but now he feels irritation and wishes she would disappear. He is described as fortunate, rich, and of the great world, yet feels powerless and isolated. A girl pleads with him, lamenting her lack of freedom and the pain of labor, while a boy, Gallegher, runs from police, feels guilty and physically distressed, and experiences sharp pains and a warm salt tear, despite being half-frozen and not doing anything wrong.

The narrator, observing a group of three girls—two younger and one elder with long hair—on a bench in a park, notes their interest in the Lohengrin swan-boats, which he considers idiotic. The younger girls express fascination with the view from the boats, particularly the island's wildness, while the elder girl suggests bears and wild animals live there. The youngest girl specifically claims the island is very wild, citing Eddie Case’s account of seeing fish, ducks, and snakes. Van Bibber, initially cross and somnolent from the heat, is drawn into their conversation, buys tickets for all three, and offers them rides. His brother jokes about his travels and introduces him to the girls from Hester Street, who smile kindly. Van Bibber reflects on the absurdity of swan-boat rides, noting they cost more than a car trip, and the youngest girl expresses a desire to ride once, prompting the elder girl’s reproach.

The stranger, marked by troubled eyes and a face concealed by a coat collar, travels through Philadelphia, avoiding detection by fleeing to Torresdale, a station just outside the city. He is pursued by Gallegher, who follows after giving him a hundred-yard start. The stranger enters the Eagle Inn, a roadside hostelry now serving as a hub for pothunters and a site of cock-fights, where Gallegher lets him go and seeks young Keppler, whose offspring was found in the wood-shed. Gallegher, trembling and suffering from nausea caused by fear of failure in his adventure, reflects on the loneliness of his journey and the city’s yellow glow from Philadelphia. The only significant news is the Burrbank murder, widely reported from New York to Bombay, while a minor fight near Philadelphia is noted. The stranger’s movements and appearance resemble the murderer Hade, and he is accompanied by a silent, white-faced young man who would be piloted to the Jersey shore to avoid police surveillance.

Stephen S. Hade, the secretary, murdered the city editor and stole $200,000 in bonds, stocks, and money from a safe accessible only to him and the editor. Hade, who lost his trigger finger as a boy, wears gloves to hide it, stuffing it with cotton to make it appear whole; he will be caught the first time he removes the glove. The city editor initially suggested looking for a tough, but Gallegher correctly reasoned that Hade would dress as a gentleman and wear gloves. Gallegher noticed a smoothly shaven man with a walking stick whose fourth finger stood out, matching Hade’s missing finger, leading him to pursue the man. Hade is believed to have fled to New York or New Jersey or taken passage from a smaller seaport. The murderer remains uncaught despite multiple arrests. Gallegher, a young man known for his cheerfulness and ability to amuse others, recognized the man and pursued him, confirming the connection.

The old man, imprisoned and sent back for twenty years to a cold, forsaken hole, has not seen his wife or daughter for seven years; his wife moved west after his imprisonment and took another name, while his daughter believes he is away at sea. The man, now returning to the West, had intended to live straight and raise money for the fare, but now believes it makes little difference. He is visited by Mr. Wolfe, who questions him about his state and his son’s absence, and later by Snipes, who dismisses the city as "unclean, wicked." The man is sent back to the West, where he meets his wife at a saloon, and they share a quiet moment amid the cold morning air. Mr. Wolfe, who refuses to act on the old man’s assault, tells him to go home to his wife and avoid drinking raw whiskey. The man’s return is marked by emotional tension and a sense of loss, as he reflects on his separation from family and the moral ambiguity of his actions.

Abraham, identified as the son of an old man, denies accusations of murder and theft, claiming he took $200 to buy a ring, which he shows in a velvet box as pretty. The old man, Abraham’s father, believes Abraham was murdered rather than a thief and questions his actions. Walter, who has followed and observed the master closely, seems to spy on him and is involved in handling his debts. The master, once at the height of his fortune, feels intense pain and decides to end his life in Monte Carlo, taking the first train there after being disinherited. While sleeping, he whispers of returning to Harringford and the governor, and speaks of a boy who came to him and ran to meet him. The master is seen sleeping peacefully, smiling, and is awakened by Walters. A ring is central to several scenes, including a performance in a barn where Gallegher dances in a sawdust-covered ring. Harringford recognizes the yellow station and great hotels upon arrival in Monte Carlo.

The narrative centers on a man navigating loneliness and emotional turmoil in a post-Parisian setting. He drives through a desolate, industrial landscape, finding fleeting comfort in the quiet activity of station operators. At the Casino, he decides against writing letters to his father or her, fearing they would be misunderstood or misused; the letters he reads are filled with bitterness and financial grievances, though his father’s final one offers peace and a welcome home, making it especially painful. He orders a woman—identified by a red coral brooch as a non-regular visitor—to leave Monte Carlo immediately, ensuring she keeps her wealth and never returns. The final *coup*, the Grand Prix and the English horse, depends on his return of fortune, reconciliation with his father, and the possibility of reuniting with her. He observes the race, fails to find the English horse, and later receives a message from the girl he knew to go to the stables, suggesting a potential reward for his care of young women.

The bishop's study resembles a man’s room devoted to books and travel imagery, reflecting his intellectual and aesthetic interests. Latimer, a young man, is deeply affected by the emotional and moral weight of a hypothetical situation, questioning the justice of judging a person’s character under impossible conditions. He is drawn to the older man, feels guilty as though robbing him, and is anxious to return to a woman he loves, whom he sees as beautiful and noble. The girl, in contrast, values boldness and happiness in love, asserting that loving a girl makes one fearless and joyful, and expresses disappointment at marrying a man who is frightened. She plays the piano in the drawing-room, a space where she controls the atmosphere by pulling and opening curtains. The young man finds happiness in proposing marriage, though he worries about the bishop’s greater ambitions for her, which are described in books. Meanwhile, Gallegher, a non-reputable but admired figure, responds to a fire at Woolwich Mills by ringing the alarm and leading the Black Diamonds against the Wharf Rats.

LITTLE BABY struggled to its feet and ran toward Raegen, holding out both bare arms with confidence and welcome. Raegen responded by gently closing the baby’s fingers in his own, and the baby smiled and laughed joyfully, sharing a good joke with Raegen. The baby is described as well pleased and appears to be in a state of happy, innocent engagement. In contrast, RAGS, a young tough, initially speaks in terror and horror, claiming self-defence after being threatened with a gun, but later shifts to a calm, evil cunning demeanor, drawing on street experience and acting with detached resolve. A boy experiences worsening head pain and nervous twitching, fearing his head may have grown longer and spongy, and is pitied for having too much heart and not enough money, making him vulnerable to exploitation. Young Latimer believes the speaker knows much about his life and family, and feels essential to seeing Miss Ellen daily, stating he cannot visit as often unless engaged to her or as her husband.

The sporting editor believes tomorrow's news will be the most important in the country and writes a letter to Michael E. Dwyer, then travels by cab to the old Eagle Inn near Torresdale, enduring a miserable night with freezing rain and snow. He sends his message to the *Press* office, lights a cigar, and curls up in the cab, while Gallegher, excited by anticipation, watches the cigar burn out. During a drive through the city on Broad Street, Gallegher narrowly avoids a confrontation with police, who whistle to stop him. The night features a brutal fight between two boxers, described as one of the bitterest in history, with the crowd in silent excitement and the master of ceremonies attempting to enforce order. The sporting editor later meets Gallegher at his home, claiming to have found the murderer, and praises Gallegher’s role in securing a $5,000 reward. Meanwhile, Rags Raegen, a man skilled in the water, is seen in a quiet, shivering state, and a baby is comforted by him, bringing him deep contentment.

Ted Standish, the younger of two sons from a Boston family, appears gloomy and disinterested during a meal, recognizing Van Bibber, his elder brother’s friend. The girl sees Ted’s brother in a hansom and exclaims, “Ted, O Ted!”; Van Bibber intervenes, claiming they are en route to Jersey City and then Chicago, where they will stay at the Palmer House. The elder Standish doubts this, as the cab driver confirms they arrived no more than half an hour ago. A tarnished silver medal, once a half-dollar, engraved with “From Henry Burgoyne to his beloved friend Lewis L. Lockwood” and “Through prosperity and adversity,” is found in a pawnbroker’s window among razors and Bibles. Miss Catherwaight, seeing a similar name, asks the groom to find Lewis Lyman Lockwood, who is located on Broadway near Liberty. Van Bibber, acting as best man, organizes the wedding, warns of a fatal mistake in marrying without proper witnesses or certificates, and plans to publicize the event as orthodox and smart. He later reflects that a man unskilled in lying should avoid deception, as demonstrated by the elder Standish’s confusion.

Gallegher, a detective with deep knowledge of criminal characters, is a key reporter who demonstrates investigative skill by exposing mismanagement at a home for orphans and later aiding in the arrest of Hade. He is entrusted with a notebook containing notes on his work, Hade’s capture, and a description of a fight, which he retrieves after being delayed and arrested. The managing editor, initially doubtful, ultimately approves publication of the story, believing a story must have been brought to the office already. The night editor argues against delay, citing financial risk, but the managing editor dismisses the possibility of failure, asserting that Dwyer would have reported a story if it existed. Gallegher is told to reach the press office by twenty minutes to three to beat the town; if he arrives on time, he will outpace both the paper and the country. The managing editor, after receiving the notebook, distributes it to reporters and comforts Gallegher, who, despite resistance, submits to his care. Gallegher instructs Hefflefinger to arrest Hade using a burglar’s warrant and transport him to New York on the owl train, ensuring the prisoner’s true identity remains secret.

Naseby, a man who described the country as attractive and improbable, left Cherry Street and returned to work in the countryside, contributing to Snipes' moroseness. An old countryman, who appears bewildered and anxious, visits Case's tenement, claiming Perceval—a man known as Alf Wolfe—sends wickedness to the country and ruined his son by allowing city children to visit his farm, where they rode horses, swam in the river, shot crows, and ate cherries. The old man saw his son reading a note as if it were Gospel. A stranger, seeking a young man resembling him with lightish hair, tall and lanky, carrying a shiny black bag, suspects he visited Perceval. Snipes, who reports such sightings to Alf Wolfe and receives a quarter, waits for another victim and a signal from No. 8. The young man proposes marrying in the Park using a borrowed coach, suggesting they return to ask the bishop’s blessing on their knees, though the girl rejects the idea as flippant. The old deacon will not allow the marriage until Abe has $2,000, and the boy intends to buy bad money to show the deacon, implying the marriage would never be happy.

The young man, Latimer, refuses to answer the bishop’s question about marrying Ellen, asserting he would be unworthy of himself and the bishop’s daughter, and claims he did not answer despite the bishop’s assertion that his silence implied a response. The bishop, observing Latimer’s hesitation, notes that a more direct expression—“Ellen is the only woman who has the power to make me happy”—would have satisfied him but was not spoken. Latimer later expresses deep love for Ellen, stating it surpasses all else and that words cannot make it truer, though she rejects him. The father, upon seeing Ellen, exclaims in pain and pity, and she responds by moving to him, hiding her face on his shoulder, exhausted and emotionally drained. The father reflects on the Prodigal Son, realizing his son is farther from him than ever, and sees the father in the story as one who runs to meet his son when far away. Ellen, the daughter, is central to the emotional core, with the father and young man both expressing love and concern for her, though she ultimately distances herself from Latimer. A door appears repeatedly as a symbol of separation or entry—opening to reveal figures or closing to isolate them—reflecting emotional thresholds.

Mr. Lockwood, who is the same person as Judge Burgoyne, is a former schoolmate and lifelong friend of another man, known for their shared past as orphans and their deep bond formed in Westchester County. He and his friend were once deeply in love with a woman, leading to a bitter quarrel and lasting separation. Lockwood is described as light-hearted, with a bright smile and energetic step, and he frequently visits the library, where he once moped after promising to go shooting but never did. He holds a medal given by a friend, which he values as a reminder of a past time, though he has a longstanding misunderstanding with the friend who gave it. The medal was found by Miss Catherwaight in a pawnshop on the Bowery, where she collected medals and stories, and she insists Lockwood keep it as a symbol of true friendship. A gold medal was awarded to Hiram J. Stillman in 1888 for saving a ship’s crew, and another was given to Colonel James F. Placer by his regiment. Lockwood once bought a Victoria Cross for five pounds, which he later felt guilty about keeping, and it was sold in London for silver. The Bowery is a central location where medals are traded and stories are told.

The Plunger, a young man with a numb, detached mindset, observes a Frenchman who insists on betting all his money on red, believing he will win a grand coup that will pay off his debts and restore his social standing. The Plunger warns him against risking everything, suggesting a safer split of 12,000 francs among three parties—himself, his wife, and the Frenchman—each betting on different outcomes. Despite this, the Frenchman continues to bet on red, which wins repeatedly, leading him to believe he will win all his money in one grand coup. The Plunger catches him by the wrists during a spin, and when the ball settles on seven, the croupier announces "red, odd, and below," confirming the Frenchman’s win. The Plunger claims he has won over 20,000 francs, congratulates him, and takes the money, placing it in the woman’s skirt. The Frenchman, initially resistant, becomes ecstatic and insists on doubling his winnings, but the Plunger blocks him. Later, the Plunger reflects on his own life, recognizing the words "you have made us happy for the rest of our lives" as matching those from his father’s letter, prompting a moment of emotional longing.

Mr. Dwyer, a sporting editor at the Press, informed Gallegher that a boy had found Hade, who would be at the fight that night, and proposed that Gallegher arrest the boy secretly using his papers and badge, pretending the boy was a burglar, and transport him on the train at 1.20 p.m. to New York, where he would receive $500 from a $5,000 reward if no one suspected the boy’s true identity. Mr. Dwyer was involved in a confrontation with Captain Scott, who refused to release him, claiming he had been put under bonds to maintain peace and that their presence was not optional. Mr. Dwyer argued that their presence was professional and that they had no right to be detained, and he was physically confronted by Captain Scott, who shoved him into officers’ hands. The green-goods men, who sell counterfeit bills for $500 in exchange for $5,000 worth of fake money, operate through letters and meetings in New York’s drug- or cigar-store post-offices, contributing to vice and crime. Captain Scott, a police officer, led the raid and asserted his authority over the newspaper men, who claimed to represent major publications.

Detective Hefflefinger, a member of Inspector Byrnes's staff, arrives in Philadelphia to arrest a burglar, Arlie Lane (alias Carleton), but the burglar has already fled. Hefflefinger later participates in a plan with Gallegher and Dwyer to arrest Hade, the Burrbank murderer, at a scheduled fight in a barn. The fight, costing $250 per ticket, is set up by Keppler, who reveals a window accessible via a wooden shutter that can be opened with a boost. Gallegher and the detective use a method involving a ladder-like boost to access the window, while Dwyer ensures the arrest remains secret to avoid local police interference or media exposure. The detective, holding Hade, threatens to reveal his true identity if he does not behave like a burglar, and after Hade's calm resistance, Hefflefinger attacks him. A man with a cape-coat arrives at the location one day prior, described as stuck-up and citified, wearing gloves, and initially claiming fear of the fight, though he later jokes about attending. Hefflefinger agrees to Dwyer’s plan, calling it a "very pretty piece of work," and later meets Gallegher at the Torresdale station to coordinate the arrest.

The boy, after coming into money, plunged into gambling and secretly backed a horse, reducing the odds against it from 60 to 0 to 6 to 0. He remembered black and larger specks at the starting-post and remained still with his feet on the wheel, back against the box-seat, hands in his pockets. Gallegher, a local resident, moves into a dark corner of a yard filled with three police patrol-wagons, each packed with unwilling passengers exposed to sleet and rain. He crawls between horses' hoofs and behind carriage wheels to a cab he placed at the furthermost gate, where the horse has its head turned toward the city. The cab’s hitching strap, covered in ice, takes him several minutes to loosen with his teeth. He climbs onto the wheel, experiences a shock of fear that causes him to lose his breath and gaze into the darkness. An officer uses a swinging light to search among carriages, and after questioning a boy who claims his father, Keppler, is in a patrol-wagon, the officer allows him to pass. Gallegher later drives the cab recklessly through desolate countryside, encountering other cabs and men who accuse him of stealing it, and eventually reaches a destination where he sees electric lights and a clock showing half-past two, prompting him to urge his horse into a gallop.

The room contains etchings, plaster casts, hundreds of books, dark red curtains, an open fire lighting brass pots with ferns, and blue and white plaques on the bookcase. The bishop sits at his writing-table, shaded by a red-covered lamp, and is described as having a strong face with white hair, yet considered young for his high office; he is wise, engaging, and has seen much trouble. A woman murmurs to a child, praising its beauty and noting it is half-starved and poorly cared for, instructing the reserve squad to retrieve milk from an ice-chest, send for a surgeon, and crack ice for the cooler. Raegen, fearing for the child, asks if the woman will die and is questioned by the group; he asserts he was not taken but chose to give himself up, a moment marked by the baby’s cheek touching his own. The surlly old sergeant, dozing under gas-jet lights, initially mocks the young man who enters with a sick baby, claiming the child is from the heat and starving, but eventually sounds the gong for the janitress. The char-woman, upon seeing the baby, runs to it, calling it a poor little thing and beautiful. The reserve squad enters leisurely with playing-cards and pipes. Wade and Heffner, ward detectives, enter from the street, looking hot, tired, and anxious.

Snipes, a small and patient trailer for the green-goods men led by Mr. Alf Wolfe, works quietly in the shadows, observing people and earning a quarter of a dollar per victim. He is proud of his role, remaining unnoticed even in crowded areas. The old man, who visits him on the stoop, is weak, troubled, and believes seeing Perceval before his son can resolve his crisis. He accuses Wolfe of luring honest boys to his den and murdering them, demanding his son be returned. When the old man claims his son is in room No. 8 of Case’s tenement, Snipes chases him, but finds the room empty. The countryman is watched by the trailer, who may take him to a private saloon where he is robbed in a manner suited to thieves’ purposes. Snipes, despite his moral conflict, remains committed to his duties, showing personal danger and internal struggle when faced with the child’s fate.

Peace was absent at home and everywhere else. The old man offered the young boy a return to a farm with cows and a river, where he could live freely and avoid the unclean, wicked city. The boy, who had been allowed to do as he wished and had faced hardship including sleeping in hallways and warm cellars, was praised as a good boy for saving his sibling from thieves. The farm, with its cows and river, represented a contrast to the city’s noise—car bells, cabs, drivers, and the rush of a metropolis—where peace was unattainable. The boy would never again see the city, which was described as chaotic and devoid of peace. The old man, happy with the boy’s actions, believed he had truly meant to save his sibling and waited in silence with him. The boy’s life mirrored those who beg or steal, and he had been repeatedly tried to be made "good" by children’s societies, which Snipes opposed. The speaker rejected hypothetical extreme conditions, asserting they could never happen to sane, healthy people.

Young Harringford, known as the "Goodwood Plunger," arrived in Monte Carlo in a state of emotional withdrawal, likened to a wounded lion or poisoned rat retreating to solitude. He stood in the Casino, watching the flaming lamps with painful seriousness, waiting for their extinction as if condemned to die at sunrise. He recalled his youth, when he and young Norton spoke daily of Siren, a horse in Norton’s father’s stables that would win the Goodwood Cup. The boy on Siren’s back, who had often been seen on the downs, was the same one who gently touched her. When Siren won, Lord Norton cried "Siren wins!" and the mob and hills echoed the name, lifting Young Harringford into a sudden sense of euphoria after three months of purgatory. Meanwhile, the people in the house had learned to direct inquiring visitors to the gentleman who rented Room No. 8, where Wolfe was to give a signal; the old man, dressed in heavy black broadcloth with home-made linen, was denied entry and complained to Snipes, who replied "Nop."

Young Raegen dove off Wakeman's Slip, swam back to the landing-steps, and pushed through the crowd to plunge into the river to rescue a supposedly drowned man, fabricating that he had touched the body in the mud. This fiction led the river-police to drag the river-bed for four hours, with Rags directing their movements from the wharf. Later, after striking McGonegal, who fell as a result, Raegen fled to the roofs for refuge. He encountered ward detectives standing on the opposite side of the street, who had been joined by two of McGonegal's friends, whom he initially believed were investigating him due to his actions. Raegen later expressed relief and rubbed perspiration from his eyes and forehead. Meanwhile, one group of neighbors laughed and talked on the roofs, playing accordion and being described as noisy and drunken fools, prompting Rags to curse them and hope they would fall off and break their necks.

Rags falls headlong over a bucket with a broom stuck in it on the fourth floor, experiencing a jolt and exhaustion from a prior race, and stumbles down narrow stairs cautiously, remembering a previous fall. He is pursued in a maze-like tenement district, where safe passages may lead to officers’ hands. A newsboy shouts the evening paper’s full account of Pike McGonegal’s murder by Ragsey Raegen, causing Rags to become blind and dizzy, and he yells "Stop" and "Murdered, no, by God, no," but no one hears him. The officer with the lantern appears behind a carriage, stands still, and peers directly at Rags, making him feel certain of being seen. Pike McGonegal, the hero of Thirty-third Street, is dead, and Rags, unaware of the danger, enters a dark room and hides under bedding, listening to footsteps and voices of two men questioning each other. The man who cared for the child expresses self-reproach and calls the woman a hulking big loafer. Footsteps clatter down the stairs, and the big house becomes silent.

The woman, Miss Catherwaight, and her husband Louis, married since Tuesday and given only three days before returning to Paris, visit a secluded spot off the drive where they once met secretly beneath a bush of box. Louis, an apprentice to Old Carbut the baker and owner of a third of his store, believes he should live with the best and play like others, though he only plays dominos at cafes. The store may be sold for 20,000 francs, after which the couple will own it fully, having saved money to buy the remaining third in five or six years. The woman finds Louis’s desire to win more and buy additional shares foolish and wicked. She remembers their past meetings, including a time when she pretended an iron grating was a radiator, and decides to bury her engagement ring in the spot as a symbol of abnegation, only to see her brougham drawn up nearby, signaling Louis’s arrival. Her brougham, a source of neighborhood delight, always has a groom standing at the door, within call.

Miss Catherwaight, a central figure, is described as unusually silent during family dinner and later believes she is the recipient of a visit from Mr. Lewis L. Lockwood, whom she met at his office to return a keepsake found in an old curio shop. The keepsake, bearing Lockwood’s name, had been stolen and pawned. She confidently asserts she will see him, though Morris is uncertain whether Lockwood came for her or Mr. Catherwaight. Mr. Catherwaight, who prefers to nap after dinner, recalls that young Lockwood was once very attentive to his mother, a detail he shares drowsily, prompting Miss Catherwaight to question the nature of that attentiveness. The mother, regarded as second only to her birth in importance, died after a great effort, remembered fondly by peers. Gallegher, another character, sometimes walks home or takes rides on a newspaper delivery wagon with damp papers. The book *Gallegher and Other Stories* by Richard Harding Davis, illustrated by Charles Dana Gibson and copyrighted in 1891 by Charles Scribner's Sons, is dedicated to the mother.

One of the reporters, reflecting on urban life, stated he has never seen anything unexplained by crime, poverty, or drink, and believed strange or romantic events ultimately resolve to known causes. He recalled Dickens’s account of a ragged man crouching under a window of the great house at the corner of the avenue and cross-street during a ball, where a woman dropped a bouquet into the man’s hand, who then ran off with it—calling this scene "really curious." The reporter noted that in a large city like this, one might expect to find mysteries such as Stevenson’s Suicide Club, but he has not. The group visited the Owl’s Nest, Gus McGowan’s all-night restaurant on Third Avenue, where they ate a perfectly done porterhouse steak. McGowan, who fell asleep behind the bar, briefly woke to a woman begging for a drink and later expelled three insolent men who had tried to force drinks. The great house faced the avenue, with a stone wall extending to a brown stone stable on the side street.

Margaret, a baby, is described as content with Rags' company, though she appears dubiously at times, causing Rags to feel guilty and anxious. She ignores Raegen’s question about her father and is unaware that her father and "mar" are serving time on the island and will not be seen for a month. Raegen mocks her strength and tells her this, but she does not care. Rags blames himself for leaving Margaret alone in the heat, calling himself a "drunken fool," and fears she may be unresponsive, though she is breathing softly. He later decides to live alone, believing he is not meant for marriage and that his experience with Margaret taught him to find amusement and occupation in life, which he will carry forward. A man with gloves on is sought by a speaker, who advises approaching him by shaking hands, gripping his forefinger (if it feels like wadded cotton), and grabbing his throat with the left hand while hollering for help. The forefinger and throat are key physical points in this instruction.

The speaker, a young man with strong self-respect, values integrity over youthful pleasures and has lived a disciplined life, avoiding dissipation despite once envying others' indulgences. He believes in a future of contentment, honor, and long-term stability, including career milestones like becoming a judge and sending his son to college. The bishop praises him, affirming a fair promise for his daughter’s future, noting he can provide her with greater pleasures, broader experiences, and more power for good, while assuring her life will be easier and more fulfilling. The bishop expresses confidence in the young man’s treatment of his daughter, Ellen, though he questions whether he can protect her from the past. The young man is concerned that his past may negatively affect her, but asserts he has maintained self-respect throughout. A separate incident involves a young couple seen as runaways, who remain unbothered by their surroundings, while a girl expresses fear at their dining arrangement, prompting Van Bibber to intervene at a church.

Rags cared for a baby in a tenement who exhibited symptoms of distress—hard, irregular breathing, open mouth, clenched fists, and deep blue rings around her eyes—resembling infants seen during Health Board visits and ambulance transports. The baby was weak, unresponsive, and appeared to look past Rags, as if seeing something he could not perceive. Rags tried to soothe her with cool water and soaked bread, but she rejected it with reproach, deeply hurting him. The hot, dry air and sun, which rose hissing from the East River and blazed into windows, worsened the environment. Rags feared for the baby and hesitated to leave, fearing he might not have the nerve to return or to act. Gallegher, a street-savvy man with a sharp mind, could distinguish patrol-wagons, ambulances, and fire-engine gongs from a distance, reflecting the streets' role in shaping knowledge and escape. The streets themselves were described as speaking of escape and a life of ill-regulated pleasures, contrasting with the baby’s silent suffering.

Dutchy Mack is a criminal alias associated with a fight in Jersey City involving the Black Diamond, a Black man known professionally as a criminal. Abe Hubbard, alias "Jimmie the Gent," is a burglar who broke jail in New Jersey and was traced to New York; detectives have a clue about his whereabouts but fear his associates will help him escape west. Van Bibber, who attended a dance the previous night and saw his name listed among attendees, learns of these events through a newspaper report. He visits his rooms, which he finds cheerless and used only for dressing and sleeping, and reflects on his life being tied to his house on Twenty-Seventh Street. He goes to Jersey City to attend a "go" between Dutchy Mack and the Black Diamond, which occurs after 2 o'clock when the backer throws a sponge into the air and they reach the city at 3 o'clock. Van Bibber walks in cold weather, feeling as if he has lost a day, and later notices his name in the newspaper regarding the dance. Gallegher knows details about Dutchy Mack’s imprisonment and aliases.

A bass voice suggests a man may be inside a dark room, which the men enter and halt at the entrance to, where they stand for over an hour before leaving, during which Raegen feels his agony is being contemplated. One of the men claims he was there twelve hours prior, having come to take a couple out for fighting; the couple yelled "murder" and "police" and broke things in the room. The man and his wife regularly got drunk and came up here, receiving thirty days on the island. The bass voice asks who takes care of the rooms, and the first voice says no one does, as there is little to maintain. In another scene, a gay party finds a body under a bush, mistaken for a dog or man asleep; one man touches it and says, "Take those girls away," and the body is later identified as a young Russian who lost badly at the tables. In a separate incident, Rags tries to feed a baby with a mixture of ham, bread crumbs, and whiskey, but the baby refuses and says it isn't any use. Rags believes the tenement residents are asleep and plans to "lift" their breakfast, but finds all rooms open and bare. The three little girls use up their tickets quickly, become sunburned, and dream of a big white swan and a young man in patent-leather boots and baggy breeches. They place an awful lunch basket on the front seat.

The Avenue stretched north and south, illuminated by a double line of flashing lights from cabs and carriages moving toward Latimer and shining at cross-streets, creating a bustling, mysterious atmosphere. Latimer stood looking toward the north with a reckless, harassed expression not seen in many months, then descended the steps quickly, stating that a commitment would last many years, and turned his back to the north, walking slowly home. A man, possibly Latimer or Gallegher, came down the steps, pulled at his gloves, and turned toward the north, feeling elation from being free and his own master, yet also a sense of littleness over having acted meanly or unworthily, believing his actions were quixotic. He tried to make it seem like she had broken with him, not him with her. A young man announced his love to Ellen, who agreed to marry him if the bishop does not oppose it, expressing deep love and a desire to make her happy despite feeling unworthy. A strange feeling caused shivering and fear of mental collapse, occurring more frequently recently. Night in a great city is described as sodden, brutal, exciting, and repetitive, with old plots, motives, and characters.

Rags is deeply engaged by an innocent entertainment involving a baby whose face is illuminated by an electric lamp; he nearly forgets he is hiding from unfriendly neighbors and authorities. The baby reaches into Rags’s shirt collar, pulls out his scapular, and looks at it with apparent seriousness, leading Rags to believe the child is a superhuman agent, a belief he struggles to reconcile with the fact that the angel’s parents live on Blackwell’s Island. A man, referred to as "the gentleman," helps a couple escape from a wretched place by taking them to a train, promising they will never return, and they express gratitude and excitement, with the woman expressing desire for his visit to Paris. The husband and daughter, after their mother’s death, live together and rarely go out, entertaining through dinners that serve as a social credential, with the daughter’s coming out being a major social effort by her mother, Miss Catherwaight, who lived solely for society and left her husband standing in drawing-rooms, where he appeared courteous but inwardly unhappy. Miss Catherwaight believes her mother was young when an accident occurred and did not know of it, and she would have acted to make it right.

The crowd, mostly composed of well-fed club-men, brokers, a politician, a comedian with his manager, amateur boxers, and quiet sporting men from across the country, gathered at an event where two disreputable men in high hats arrived in a carriage and were noted for their patent-leather boots. They were rumored to be funding the Black Diamond against Hester Street Jackson, earning respect among spectators. The crowd cheered when the men tossed their high hats into the ring, interpreting it as a sign the fight was beginning. Hade, a man in deep anxiety, hid his pale face beneath a cloth cap and woolen scarf, fearing danger from the already suspicious Keppler. He came to the event because staying away would have made his danger greater. Gallegher waited two hours, tense and fearful of police raids or delays, especially concerning Mr. Dwyer’s timely return. Perspiration stood out on the backs of the backers, and spectators shouted names like "Firefly" and "Vixen" as horses entered the stretch, while one man waited to see the Norton colors before speaking.

The office employs office boys who, before Gallegher joined, lost individuality and were categorized as sleepy, lazy, or bright and smart, eventually leaving the office due to familiarity, becoming district-messenger boys or returning in blue coats with nickel-plated buttons to patronize the office. Mr. Latimer, the junior partner, is a dancing acquaintance of Miss Catherwaight and briefly assists her when Mr. Lockwood is out, though he appears surprised and overdoes his efforts, making her realize her visit is unusual. A man in the office has responsibility for a boy, will say the word to prevent the office boys from approaching him, and will steer the boy to the old man at the Grand Central Depot, where the old man is told to wait. The man’s sympathy overcomes his judgment, and he refuses to answer questions, warning the old man not to get into trouble. Raegen, having shaken the gang, believes his family was better off after the Society deemed them unfit to care for her, and despite being imprisoned, he receives daily visits from her, who kisses him through the bars.

The protagonist, once known as Young Van Bibber, experienced periods of fortune and greater fortune, returning to crowded inns, sunburnt and fagged from excitement, where he indulged in riotous suppers and baccarat, sleeping only to see cards, horses, crowds, and dust clouds. He wore a short covert coat with a field-glass and a pasteboard ticket. A change brought back his conscience, leading to visits to the Jews and a sense of moral regret. He then faced debts, more debts, borrowed money to pay obligations, and threats of executions. He longed for the fields, trout springs, and Surrey, particularly for the walk across the park to where a girl lived. Young Van Bibber came to town in June from Newport to see his lawyer about signing papers, finding the city hot, close, dreary, and empty. He criticized unchaperoned drives through the park as very bad form, though he acknowledged the engagement. He also remarked that if Miss Catherwaight disliked dances, days, or teas, she should stop attending rather than make unpleasant remarks. He lost his former status, his right to sit at his father's table, and the girl’s lighted window in the north wing, becoming known as "the Goodwood Plunger" — a man mocked by fortune and conscience.

Cecil is deeply cherished by the speaker, who describes him as the "flesh of my flesh and the bone of my bone," and states that he cannot live or find rest—either in this life or the next—without him. Cecil is the source of the speaker’s heartaches and insomnia, and he is essential for the speaker to hear, see, and touch. At a French restaurant near Washington Square, Van Bibber observes a young lady and a young gentleman at a table next to him; the young lady is described as very young, very pretty, and in a highly excited state, wearing a wide-brimmed pointed French hat and patent-leather ties. Van Bibber has lunch there after waiting for an afternoon train and is glad he came, noting the cool breeze and the absence of dust or horse-car bells. A burglar is allowed to rob Van Bibber’s house the next night under strict instructions: bags must be placed in the kitchen door, the burglar must walk ahead of Van Bibber toward Grand Central Station, keep hands in pockets, and not run, as Van Bibber has the burglar’s pistol. Van Bibber feels guilty as he passes police but regains composure by thinking of his wife and child in the West. Cecil, upon returning home, finds his servant tearing up a letter to his father and decides to leave immediately, taking the first train.
